faqs.q: A raccoon is denning in my Cumberland chimney — how is that handled?
faqs.a: Chimneys are a favorite spring den in Cumberland's older brick housing, especially around Washington Street and the hillside blocks above Wills Creek. We first check whether pups are present, because a mother separated from her litter will tear at flashing and mortar trying to get back in. The family comes out together whenever possible, and Maryland law does not allow raccoons to be relocated, so the work ends with exclusion and a properly fitted chimney cap rather than a release somewhere else. Once the cap and any damaged crown or flashing are dealt with, that flue stops being an annual den.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Cumberland?
faqs.a: In Cumberland the number turns mostly on access and on how the houses connect. A single squirrel entry on a detached La Vale-style ranch is a different job from a raccoon family in a shared rowhouse chimney downtown, where sealing has to account for the neighboring rooflines as well. Steep hillside lots, slate or metal roofs, and bat colonies in larger older homes each change the scope. We inspect the roofline, attic, and foundation first, walk you through the droppings, damage, and entry points we found, and give you the full figure before removal or sealing starts — nothing is priced sight unseen over the phone.

Cumberland.wildlife_intro:
Cumberland grew up where Wills Creek cuts through the Narrows and meets the North Branch of the Potomac, and that tight valley geography shapes the wildlife work here. Brick rowhouses and steep hillside streets climb away from the canal basin and the old railroad yards, giving raccoons easy travel along retaining walls, fences, and connected rooflines. Uncapped chimneys on the older Washington Street and Greene Street stock are classic spring den sites, and a female raccoon with pups in a flue is one of the most common April calls in the city.

The ridges on both sides of town hold bats through the summer, and big brown bats slip into the gable ends and church belfries of the older neighborhoods when evenings warm. Groundhogs work the sunny banks along the C&O Canal towpath and the rail embankments, while skunks den under the porches of hillside homes where the yards step down in terraces. Copperheads use the rocky, sun-warmed slopes above the river, and every snake call here is handled as a careful non-lethal capture with release on site or close by, exactly as Maryland requires. In Cumberland the fix is rarely one hole: connected rowhouses mean the entry on your roof may belong to a gap two doors down, so the whole run of rooflines gets checked before anything is sealed.

faqs.q: I hear scratching in my Frostburg attic at night — what could it be?
faqs.a: Night-only scratching in Allegany County often means bats, flying squirrels or raccoons, while daytime running usually points to gray squirrels. Around Rocky Gap State Park, the cover close to housing means several species are plausible, so call us for an inspection and we will identify the animal before anything is sealed.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Frostburg porch?
faqs.a: Keep dogs inside at dusk and do not try to block the opening while the skunk is home — that traps it and guarantees a spray. Our crew removes skunks from under porches and decks in Frostburg with covered, low-stress handling, then screens the opening so the next skunk cannot move in.

faqs.q: Squirrels keep getting into my La Vale attic every fall — why here?
faqs.a: La Vale's subdivisions sit right against the Haystack Mountain ridges, and the mature oaks in yards along the National Road corridor drop acorns over the roofs each autumn. Gray squirrels follow that food, then look for attic warmth as nights cool, entering at gable vents, soffit returns, and spots where branches touch the roof. We remove the squirrels using one-way exits, screen the vents with heavy-gauge material squirrels cannot chew through, and point out the branches worth trimming back. Sealing only the hole you can see rarely works here because the same roofline usually has two or three chewed entries.

faqs.q: What does a bat job involve in a La Vale home?
faqs.a: Bat work in Maryland is exclusion only — no lethal methods — and La Vale's ridge-side homes get summer colonies of big brown bats in attic peaks and behind shutters. We map every entry gap, fit one-way exits, and seal the rest of the roofline so the colony leaves on its own and cannot re-enter. Timing matters: Maryland DNR recommends the September 1 to March 1 window, and colonies of more than 10 adults need prior approval from the Service to exclude between March 1 and August 31, when flightless pups may be present. We will tell you plainly if your colony has to wait for the safe window.

La Vale.wildlife_intro:
La Vale spreads along the National Road corridor west of Cumberland, where postwar subdivisions climb the lower slopes of Haystack Mountain and back up to wooded ridges. That suburb-meets-mountain edge is exactly where gray squirrels thrive: mature oaks overhang the rooflines of the ranch and split-level streets, and by late fall squirrels are testing every loose soffit and gable vent for a warm attic.

Bats follow the same ridge line, roosting behind shutters and in the attic peaks of the older homes closer to the Narrows, while groundhogs dig into the sloping back yards and under the decks that step down La Vale's hillsides. Skunks work the lawns along the creek bottoms for grubs in late summer, and homeowners near the wooded edges see opossums most nights at pet bowls left on back porches. Black rat snakes turn up in stone retaining walls and cool basements — a harmless, protected species we move only a short distance, on site or within two miles as Maryland allows. La Vale jobs usually come down to tree clearance and vent screening: when the canopy touches the roof, the animals treat the house as part of the woods, and the sealing has to prove them wrong.

faqs.q: I found a copperhead near my Westernport home — what should I do?
faqs.a: Keep people and pets inside and watch the snake from a distance so it does not slip away before help arrives. Copperheads are common on the rocky, sun-warmed slopes around Georges Creek and the Potomac, and all Maryland snakes are protected — a permitted operator may not kill them. We capture the snake without harming it and release it on site away from the house or within two miles with permission, as COMAR requires. We will also point out what drew it in, usually rock piles, woodpiles, or heavy ground cover against the foundation, so the next encounter is less likely.

faqs.q: Why do raccoons keep returning to homes in Westernport?
faqs.a: Westernport's housing climbs straight into the woods, so raccoons living along Georges Creek reach porches, trash, and chimneys within a few yards of their cover. A chimney that hosted pups one spring smells like a den the next year, and an unsealed crawlspace vent on the uphill side of a house is an open invitation. We remove the animals present — raccoons cannot be relocated under Maryland law, so on-site outcomes and exclusion are the honest tools — then cap the chimney and screen every vent and roof junction. The return visits stop when the house stops offering a den, not before.

Westernport.wildlife_intro:
Westernport sits at the far western end of Allegany County where Georges Creek meets the North Branch of the Potomac, a compact mill and railroad town pressed between steep mountainsides. Homes climb the slopes in tight rows, back yards run straight into brush and rock, and wildlife barely has to travel to reach a roofline. Raccoons den in the chimneys and crawlspaces of the older workers' housing, and skunks settle under the porches that step up the hillsides.

The paper-mill heritage left a mix of brick commercial blocks and frame houses with additions layered over a century, and every roof-to-roof junction is a potential bat entry in summer. Groundhogs burrow the sunny banks above Georges Creek and under outbuildings on the larger lots at the town edges, and copperheads use the rocky slopes and old stone walls — always a keep-your-distance call handled by non-lethal capture and short-distance release. Timber rattlesnakes belong to these same mountain ridges and are strictly a safety and referral matter, never a removal promise. In Westernport, sealing work has to respect the terrain: entries hide on the uphill side of houses where the slope meets the roof, and that is where our inspections start.
